text: Amcor plc, a public limited company incorporated under the laws of the Bailiwick of Jersey, has a history spanning more than 150 years with origins in both Australia and the United States. It is a global leader in developing and producing responsible packaging for food, beverage, pharmaceutical, medical, home and personal-care, and other products. The company’s innovation and global packaging expertise enable it to address packaging challenges worldwide by offering more functional, appealing, and cost-effective solutions for customers and consumers, while also being more sustainable for the environment. Sustainability is central to Amcor’s business and a key growth opportunity; in January 2018, it became the world’s first packaging company to pledge that all its packaging would be designed to be recycled, compostable, or reusable by 2025 and to increase the use of recycled content. Amcor delivers on these commitments through innovation and partnerships, focusing on three elements of responsible packaging: product innovation, consumer participation, and infrastructure development. The company’s product portfolio is diverse and dynamic, driven by continuous innovation and close customer partnerships, with annual investments of approximately $100 million in research and development. Amcor offers a wide range of packaging solutions across paper, metal, plastic, recycled, and bio-based materials, with expertise in the sustainable use of recyclable plastics. Its business strategy includes a focused portfolio of strong businesses in flexible and rigid packaging, specialty cartons, and closures, based on criteria such as focus on primary packaging for fast-moving consumer goods, good industry structure, attractive relative growth, and multiple paths to win through leadership, scale, and innovation. The strategy is underpinned by five core capabilities—Talent, Commercial Excellence, Operational Leadership, Innovation, and Cash and Capital Discipline—guided by values of Safety, Integrity, Collaboration, Accountability, and Results and Outperformance. Amcor generates strong cash flow and redeems it to create superior shareholder value through dividends, organic growth, and targeted acquisitions or share buybacks. According to Accounting Standards Codification (ASC) 280, the company reports two segments: Flexibles and Rigid Packaging. As of June 30, 2023, the Flexibles Segment, which operates in 37 countries with approximately 35,000 employees across 166 manufacturing and support facilities, accounted for about 76% of consolidated net sales and supplies flexible packaging globally. The Rigid Packaging Segment, employing approximately 5,000 employees at 52 facilities in 11 countries, accounted for about 24% of consolidated net sales and manufactures rigid packaging containers and related products in the Americas. Sales are primarily made through a direct sales force supported by product development engineers, design technicians, field service technicians, and customer service teams, with sales offices and plants located across Europe, North America, Latin America, Africa, and the Asia-Pacific regions. Amcor did not have sales to any single customer exceeding 10% of consolidated net sales in the last three fiscal years. Working capital varies throughout the year based on business volume and market conditions, and the company maintains inventory levels to balance favorable raw material procurement with timely order fulfillment. Manufacturing backlogs are not a significant factor in its operations. Major raw materials include polymer resins and films, paper, inks, solvents, adhesives, aluminum, and chemicals, sourced from various global suppliers, with no significant dependence on any one supplier. Although past industry-wide shortages have occurred, the company has managed supply disruptions through close collaboration with suppliers and customers. Price volatility in raw materials has occurred and has been historically linked to supply shortages, but increases in raw material costs are generally passed on to customers via contractual mechanisms. The company manages supply chain risks through relationship, inventory, and alternative sourcing evaluations. It holds over a thousand U.S. and international patents, patent applications, trademarks, and maintains certain technologies as trade secrets, which provide a competitive advantage; however, the loss of any single patent or license would not materially affect overall operations or segments. Patents, applications, and licenses expire or terminate according to their terms or by law. Sustainability is embedded throughout the business, with a focus on product innovation, consumer participation, and waste management infrastructure to meet customer demands for cost-effective, convenient, and environmentally responsible packaging. Amcor spends approximately $100 million annually on research and development (not including incremental improvements) and has over 1,000 active patents, supported by a global network of Innovation Centers. The company collaborates with customers, suppliers, NGOs, startups, and cross-industry bodies to advance recycling, reuse, and environmental performance. It has also committed to science-based targets to reduce greenhouse gas emissions and achieve net zero by 2050, with these targets submitted to the Science Based Targets initiative (SBTi) in June 2023. These efforts build on the EnviroAction program, which has improved energy, water, and waste management for over a decade. The company believes its global scale, industry experience, and capabilities position it to lead sustainable packaging development, which is a key growth opportunity. Operations and real property are subject to broad governmental laws and regulations related to employee health and safety, environmental discharge, waste handling, pollution control, and natural resource management. Amcor believes it is substantially compliant with these regulations through its Environmental, Health, and Safety Management System and regular audits, though it cannot predict future liabilities related to contamination at former or current sites or off-site disposal of regulated materials. These regulations are continually evolving, and changes cannot always be anticipated. The business is not significantly affected by seasonal factors, with cash flow typically lower in the first half and higher in the second half of the fiscal year due to working capital management and timing of payments such as incentive compensation. As of June 30, 2023, Amcor had approximately 41,000 employees worldwide, with 30% in North America, 30% in Europe, 20% in Latin America, and 20% in Asia-Pacific. Approximately 45% of the workforce is covered by collective bargaining agreements, with about 3% under expired contracts and 17% covered by agreements expiring within one year. Safety is a core value, with all facilities complying with global EHS standards; during fiscal year 2023, injuries decreased by 31%, and 69% of sites were injury-free. The company focuses on attracting, developing, engaging, and retaining top talent through a five-year Human Capital Strategy (2023–2027) to ensure the right people are in the right roles. Talent development includes executive programs such as Leading to Outperform (LTO), Senior Leader Development Program (SLDP), and a new Executive Development Program (EDP 2.0) launched in fiscal year 2023, targeting senior leaders with immersive training in strategy and talent leadership, in partnership with global academic and executive education institutions. Employees also access the "Masterclass" program, featuring annual executive briefings on functional excellence and business initiatives, with a focus in 2023 on accelerating growth through presentations from Marketing, R&D, Product Branding, and Innovation leaders. Amcor is committed to diversity, equity, and inclusion, focusing on building inclusive leadership, removing bias in talent attraction and development, and sharing best practices. Progress is reported annually to the Board, and the company works to strengthen diversity transparency while complying with privacy laws. Engagement is tracked across regions and compared to global manufacturing peers through anonymous surveys, providing feedback for continuous improvement. Ethical conduct is fundamental, with all employees required to adhere to a Code of Business Conduct and Ethics, reinforced through global training aligned with local laws. Amcor plc is subject to various risk factors that could materially affect its business, financial condition, results of operations, or cash flows. Strategic risks include changes in consumer demand, where shifts in preferences—driven by cost, economic conditions, regulations, health, environmental, or social concerns—may reduce demand for certain products or render existing ones obsolete, and new products may fail to meet sales or margin expectations due to inaccurate demand forecasting or delays in development. The company is also exposed to key customer risks, such as the loss of major customers, reductions in their production needs, or customer consolidation, which can reduce sales revenue and profitability. Customer consolidation may lead to increased pricing pressure, and despite past success in managing such changes, adverse shifts in terms or volume could harm operations. Competition remains significant across geographies and end-use sectors, with competition based on price, innovation, sustainability, service, and quality, and competitors may introduce disruptive technologies. Amcor’s growth strategy includes organic expansion through product innovation, investments, and acquisitions, but success is uncertain due to market saturation, changing customer plans, or difficulties in identifying and closing suitable acquisition targets. Investments in uncontrolled companies through corporate venturing may result in misaligned interests or future impairment losses. Integration challenges, including cultural and operational difficulties, may delay or reduce expected synergies and increase costs. Operational risks include global economic conditions, such as the Russia-Ukraine conflict and inflation, which have negatively impacted operations and may continue to do so, affecting demand, payment delays, supply chain disruptions, and profit margins. Inflation pressures are mitigated through pricing actions and productivity programs, but these may not fully offset costs. International operations expose Amcor to risks such as regulatory changes, trade restrictions, political instability, currency fluctuations, and geopolitical events, with approximately 74% of sales in fiscal year 2023 coming from developed markets and 26% from emerging markets. The Russia-Ukraine conflict has led to sanctions, supply chain disruptions, rising raw material costs, and adverse impacts on customer demand and financing. Amcor operates in countries subject to U.S. and international sanctions, requiring internal controls to avoid violations of laws related to money laundering, export controls, and economic sanctions. Raw material price fluctuations and shortages—such as those in polymer resins, paper, inks, aluminum, and energy—are influenced by inflation, currency movements, geopolitical risks, and supply chain disruptions, including the Russia-Ukraine conflict and trade policies like U.S. tariffs on Chinese aluminum and potential retroactive duties on imports from Thailand and South Korea. While Amcor uses pricing adjustments, contracts, and alternative suppliers to manage these risks, there is no guarantee of success. Commercial risks include operational disruptions from war, health crises, or supply shortages, as well as counterparty credit risks, which are heightened during economic volatility. For example, adverse weather in the U.S. in 2023 reduced cattle herds and increased meat prices, leading to lower meat packaging sales. Insolvency or default by customers, suppliers, or financial institutions could impair operations and financial health, especially during periods of economic instability.

Materials, equipment, and other supplies can negatively impact Amcor’s ability to supply products to customers. Climate change may reduce agricultural productivity, leading to availability and price challenges for agricultural commodities, which could affect demand for Amcor’s products. For example, in fiscal year 2023, adverse weather in the United States reduced cattle herds, causing meat prices to rise and resulting in lower meat packaging sales volumes. The potential magnitude of these commercial risks on Amcor’s business, financial condition, results of operations, or cash flows cannot be predicted. The insolvency or contractual default by any of Amcor’s customers, suppliers, or financial institutions—such as banks or insurance providers—could materially harm operations and financial condition, especially during periods of economic volatility, such as that caused by the Russia-Ukraine conflict. If a counterparty defaults on a payment obligation, Amcor may be unable to collect the owed amounts, which could require write-offs. If a counterparty becomes insolvent or fails to meet obligations related to a project, Amcor may need to find a replacement or fulfill the obligations itself, which would likely be more expensive. These risks could have a material adverse effect on Amcor’s business, financial condition, results of operations, or cash flows, potentially leading to a competitive disadvantage. Health crises, including pandemics, epidemics, or disease outbreaks like COVID-19, may disrupt operations through temporary facility closures, supply chain interruptions, customer shutdowns, volatility in raw material costs, and labor shortages, with broader global economic or geopolitical implications. For instance, in the first half of fiscal year 2023, the Chinese government imposed sporadic COVID-19-related lockdowns, reducing demand for Amcor’s products and disrupting global supply chains. While protocols exist to manage such impacts, the extent of health crisis effects on Amcor’s business and financial results remains unknown and could be material. Amcor’s success depends on its ability to attract, develop, and retain skilled and diverse personnel in its global executive management and operations. Although Amcor has implemented talent acquisition, onboarding, and leadership programs to align new hires with company values, failure to successfully transition key hires or retain skilled personnel could disrupt strategic execution, hinder performance objectives, and impact business continuity. Regional labor shortages, wage inflation, a competitive labor market, and demographic changes pose ongoing challenges. While Amcor has managed past labor shortages and succession planning, there is no assurance it can manage future labor issues or recruit, develop, assimilate, motivate, and retain employees who uphold company culture. Amcor is subject to environmental, health, and safety (EHS) laws and regulations in all countries where it operates, as well as local and international standards for healthcare and food packaging products. Compliance requires significant financial and human resources. Changes in workplace health and safety laws or environmental regulations—such as those related to air, soil, water quality, and climate change—can increase operational costs. Amcor may face environmental liabilities for contamination at owned, used, or operated facilities, including future acquisitions, and could be subject to fines, penalties, or mandated remediation programs requiring substantial capital expenditures. Past and future environmental fines, legal costs, damage to natural resources, lost property values, and toxic tort claims may occur. Provisions are made when it is probable that liability exists and the amount can be reasonably estimated, but actual liabilities may exceed these provisions due to the difficulty in assessing long-term environmental damage. As a result, additional charges could arise, adversely affecting operating results and financial position. Climate change and greenhouse gas emissions may negatively impact Amcor’s business, with governmental bodies considering or introducing regulatory changes that could materially affect operations or financial results. Amcor is also exposed to labor disputes and the inability to renew collective bargaining agreements at acceptable terms. Approximately 45% of its employees are covered by such agreements, and although no significant labor disputes have occurred recently, isolated work stoppages have happened. Future labor disputes, including strikes or protests, could disrupt operations and harm business performance. Amcor may also fail to renegotiate agreements at acceptable terms, despite generally good employee relations. Disruptions from labor disputes among suppliers, customers, or other parties could also affect operations. Climate change poses risks through natural disasters such as snowstorms, extreme heat, hurricanes, flooding, forest fires, deforestation, loss of biodiversity, earthquakes, and drought, which could physically damage facilities, workforce, inventory, suppliers, and equipment, leading to unplanned downtime and unabsorbed costs. Climate change may also result in higher insurance premiums or the inability to insure certain risks. Long-term climate patterns could alter customer demand, especially among those relying on weather-affected supply chains, such as agricultural supply chains impacted by drought or flooding, or coastal customers affected by frequent flooding. Amcor faces cybersecurity risks from increased cyber-attacks—including computer viruses, ransomware, unauthorized access, phishing, hacking, and advanced persistent threats—by nation-state actors, criminal enterprises, individuals, or other threat groups. These risks are heightened by geopolitical turmoil, such as the Russia-Ukraine conflict, increased work-from-home arrangements, and interconnected networks. Although Amcor has operational safeguards like employee training, network monitoring, strong data protection, and upgraded security systems, these measures cannot eliminate the risk entirely. Past and ongoing attacks may still impact systems, and business recovery protocols may not succeed, leading to material adverse effects on financial condition, results of operations, or cash flows. Customers, suppliers, and third-party service providers are also vulnerable to cyber-attacks, which could reduce demand for Amcor’s products or limit supply. Amcor holds sensitive, confidential, or personal data subject to privacy and security laws, which are evolving, especially in the U.S., Europe, and China, increasing compliance complexity and costs. Despite efforts to protect data, breaches, misplaced or lost data, programming or user errors, and malicious or accidental destruction could compromise data, lead to improper system use, and result in damages, disruptions, shutdowns, transaction errors, loss of customers, violations of privacy laws, regulatory fines, penalties, reputational damage, and compensatory payments—all of which could materially harm business and financial performance. Information technology failures or disruptions—due to power outages, software or hardware failures, cyber-attacks, natural disasters, telecommunications failures, user errors, unauthorized access, or catastrophic events—could compromise data, disrupt operations, and affect business performance. While Amcor has established and regularly tests a business disaster recovery plan, there is no guarantee it will resolve disruptions promptly. Such failures could lead to material adverse effects on business, financial condition, results of operations, and cash flows. Rising interest rates increase borrowing costs on variable-rate debt. As of June 30, 2023, approximately 30% of Amcor’s indebtedness was subject to variable interest rates. Higher inflation in Europe and the U.S. led central banks to raise interest rates during fiscal year 2023, increasing Amcor’s interest payments and potentially reducing the attractiveness of cash management programs like customer and supply chain finance, which could negatively impact cash and working capital and increase borrowings. Amcor manages interest rate exposure through a mix of fixed- and variable-rate debt, monitoring global rates, and using derivative instruments. However, if these instruments are ineffective, if Amcor is under-hedged, or if a hedge provider defaults, it could materially harm business, financial condition, results of operations, or cash flows. Continued interest rate increases could also raise the cost of obtaining new debt or refinancing existing debt. As of June 30, 2023, Amcor had $6.7 billion of debt outstanding and $1.3 billion of a $3.8 billion revolving credit facility undrawn, and it is not restricted from incurring additional debt. Amcor’s ability to service debt depends on generating sufficient cash flows, which are influenced by economic and competitive conditions and factors beyond its control. If cash flows are insufficient, financial condition and results of operations would be materially harmed. Amcor funds operations through cash from operations, commercial paper, bank term loans, committed and uncommitted credit facilities, debt issuances, and equity issuances. Credit rating agencies assess debt based on financial performance, industry outlook, and global economic conditions. Additional debt could negatively affect credit ratings, with potential outcomes including downgrades, placement on a watch list, or reduced access to capital markets, higher borrowing costs, or increased credit spreads. In addition, a significant number of Amcor’s operating subsidiaries are not guarantors of its debt. If any non-guarantor subsidiary becomes insolvent, liquidates, reorganizes, dissolves, or winds up, its assets will satisfy claims of its creditors, and there are no direct obligations to pay Amcor’s debt. Claims against such subsidiaries are structurally subordinated to all claims of their creditors. Amcor is exposed to foreign exchange rate risk, both transactional and translational. Transactional exposures arise from operations in currencies other than the entity’s functional currency, while translational exposures result from exchange rate fluctuations when converting functional currencies to U.S. dollars, affecting reported asset and liability values, income, and expenses. Movements in the exchange rates of the Euro, the United Kingdom Pound Sterling, the Swiss Franc, the Australian Dollar, the Chinese Yuan, and the Brazilian Real against the U.S. dollar may impact translational exposure. Exchange rates may change rapidly due to various factors. Amcor has recognized foreign exchange losses related to currency devaluation in Argentina, which is designated as a highly inflationary economy under U.S. GAAP. To the extent currency devaluation occurs across operations, Amcor may experience a lag in the timing to pass on these costs.

Translational foreign exchange exposures arise from exchange rate fluctuations when converting entity functional currencies to U.S. dollars, the company’s reporting currency, and may affect the reported value of assets, liabilities, income, and expenses. These exposures are particularly sensitive to movements in the exchange rates between the Euro, the United Kingdom Pound Sterling, the Swiss Franc, the Australian Dollar, the Chinese Yuan, and the Brazilian Real against the U.S. dollar. Exchange rates between transactional currencies can change rapidly due to various factors. The company has recognized foreign exchange losses related to currency devaluation in Argentina, which has been designated as a highly inflationary economy under U.S. GAAP. Refer to Note 2, "Significant Accounting Policies," of the notes to consolidated financial statements for further details on highly inflationary accounting. If currency devaluation occurs across the business, there may be a lag in passing through U.S. dollar-denominated input costs, which would negatively impact margins and profitability. As a result, the company is exposed to future exchange rate fluctuations that could materially adversely affect reported cash flow, financial condition, and results of operations. The Board of Directors has approved a hedging policy to manage such risks; however, if hedges are ineffective, if the company is under-hedged, or if a hedge provider defaults, it could materially harm cash flow, financial condition, and results of operations. Key differences between Amcor’s rights under Jersey law and Delaware corporate law include: under Jersey law, shareholders holding 10% or more of voting rights may require a special meeting, whereas Delaware law generally does not allow such a right unless granted in the certificate of incorporation or by-laws; in Delaware, a minimum quorum of one-third of issued shares is required for meetings, while Jersey law allows quorum to be set in the Articles of Association as a majority of voting rights of shareholders entitled to vote; Delaware has a business combination statute that prohibits transactions with interested shareholders for three years unless the board approves the transaction beforehand, while Jersey law does not have such a statute but prohibits business combinations with interested shareholders for three years unless the board previously approved the transaction; in Delaware, interested directors must disclose conflicts and may be held accountable if they fail to do so, while in Jersey, a transaction is not voidable if it is fair and approved by the board or shareholders.

Under Delaware corporate law, interested director transactions are permissible and not legally voidable if either a majority of disinterested directors or a majority in interest of holders of shares of the corporation’s capital stock entitled to vote approve the transaction, or if the transaction is determined to be fair to the corporation at the time it is authorized, approved, or ratified by the board of directors, a committee thereof, or the shareholders. A transaction is not voidable and a director is not accountable for failure to disclose an interest if it is confirmed by a special resolution of shareholders (requiring a two-thirds majority of those voting) and the nature and extent of the director’s interest are disclosed in reasonable detail in the notice of the meeting. Although a court may order a director to account for any profit, it will not set aside a transaction unless it is satisfied that third parties acting in good faith would not be unfairly prejudiced and the transaction was not reasonable and fair in the interests of the company at the time. Cumulative voting for director elections is not permitted under Delaware law unless specifically provided for in the corporation’s certificate of incorporation. The certificate of incorporation may allow shareholders of any class or series to vote cumulatively at all or specified elections. Under Delaware law, unless otherwise provided, shareholder actions at annual or special meetings may be taken by written consent of holders of outstanding stock with at least the minimum votes needed to pass the action at a meeting, provided all shareholders entitled to vote are present and vote; consents must be dated and collected within 60 days of the earliest dated consent. A merger, consolidation, or sale of all or substantially all assets of a Delaware corporation must be approved by the board and a majority of outstanding shares entitled to vote. Under Jersey law, a merger or consolidation of two or more companies requires the directors of each constituent company to enter into and approve a written merger agreement (in certain circumstances), which must be authorized by a special resolution of shareholders (requiring at least two-thirds of votes cast at a quorate meeting or a higher threshold as set in the articles). Dissenting shareholders of a Jersey company have no appraisal rights and cannot receive payment in cash for the judicially determined fair value of their shares, though they may object to a merger on grounds of unfair prejudice. Jersey law contains no specific restrictions on directors’ powers to dispose of company assets, but directors must act with care, in good faith, for a proper purpose, and in the best interests of the company. Directors are elected by a plurality of votes of shares entitled to vote and may be removed with or without cause (except in a classified board where removal without cause is only permitted if the certificate of incorporation provides otherwise), and require majority approval of outstanding shares. A director of a Delaware corporation has a fiduciary duty to the corporation and shareholders, consisting of a duty of care (to act with the care of a prudent person and disclose material information) and a duty of loyalty (to act in the best interests of the corporation, avoid conflicts of interest, and not use corporate position for personal gain). Delaware corporations may indemnify directors and officers against expenses, judgments, fines, and settlements incurred in defending actions if they acted in good faith and in the best interests of the corporation, or if they had no reasonable cause to believe their conduct was unlawful. Jersey law does not permit companies to limit director liability for breaches of fiduciary duty, though a Jersey company may exempt directors and officers from liability and indemnify them for liabilities such as defending civil or criminal proceedings where they are acquitted or receive a favorable judgment, where proceedings are discontinued or settled on terms involving benefit or detriment, or where the person acted in good faith with a view to the company’s best interests, or where the company maintains insurance for persons other than directors. Under English insolvency law, if a company enters administration or goes into liquidation, then the administrator or liquidator, as applicable, has certain powers to apply to the court for such order as the court sees fit (including an order to set aside any transaction) to restore the position to what it would have been if the company had not entered into a transaction with any person at an "undervalue" (as described in the UK Insolvency Act 1986) if the transaction was entered into at a time in the period of two years ending with the onset of insolvency. A transaction might be at an "undervalue" if the company makes a gift to or otherwise receives no consideration from another party or receives consideration the value of which (in money or money's worth) is significantly lower than the value of the consideration given by the company. A court generally will not intervene, however, if the company entered into a transaction in good faith and for the purpose of carrying on its business and, at the time it did so, there were reasonable grounds for believing the transaction would benefit the company. Additionally, if the liquidator or administrator can show that a "preference" was given by a company at a time in the period of six months ending with the onset of insolvency (or two years if the preference is to a connected person), a court can make such order as it sees fit to restore the position to what it would have been had the preference not been given (including an order to set aside any transaction). Generally, a company gives a preference to a person if it does anything or suffers anything to be done which has the effect of putting a person who is one of the company's creditors, sureties or guarantors in a position which, in the event of the company's insolvent liquidation, will be better than the position that person would have been in had that thing not been done. A court will only make an order in respect of a transaction at an undervalue or a preference if, at the time of the relevant transaction or preference, the company was insolvent within the meaning of the UK Insolvency Act 1986 or became insolvent as a consequence of the transaction or preference. Further, a court will not make an order in respect of a preference to a person unless the company was influenced in deciding to give the preference by a desire to improve that person's position in the event of the company's insolvent liquidation than if that thing had not been done, though this desire is presumed where the preference is to a connected person. In addition, if it can be shown that a transaction entered into by a company was made at an undervalue and was made for the purpose of putting assets beyond the reach, or otherwise prejudicing the interests, of persons who might claim against it, then the court may make such order as it thinks fit for restoring the position to what it would have been had the transaction not been entered into (including an order to set aside any transaction) and for protecting the interests of "victims" of the transaction. Any person who is such a "victim" of the transaction (with the leave of the court), as well as the administrator or liquidator of the company, may assert such a claim. There is no statutory time limit within which a claim must be made, other than relevant limitation periods, and the company need not be insolvent at the time of the transaction or in liquidation or administration. Under Australian insolvency laws, a guarantee may not be enforceable against a guarantor if a court were to find, in an insolvency or liquidation proceeding, (a) that the guarantor was insolvent (unable to pay its debts as they become due) at the time it provided its guarantee or was rendered insolvent by virtue of giving such guarantee and (b) upon application of a liquidator, where the winding up has begun within four years of the issuance of such guarantee, that the issuance of such guarantee was an "uncommercial transaction" under the Australian Act, which determination would be based upon a conclusion that a reasonable person in such guarantor's circumstances would not have issued such guarantee after consideration of (i) the benefits, if any, realized by such guarantor of issuing such guarantee, (ii) the detriment to such guarantor of issuing such guarantee, (iii) the respective benefits realized by other parties to the transaction, and (iv) any other fact that a reasonable person would consider relevant in connection with making such determination. Under United States bankruptcy law and comparable provisions of state fraudulent transfer laws, a guarantee can be voided, or claims under a guarantee may be subordinated to all other debts of that guarantor if, among other things, the guarantor, at the time it incurred the indebtedness evidenced by its guarantee: (i) intended to hinder, delay or defraud any present or future creditor or received less than reasonably equivalent value or fair consideration for the incurrence of the guarantee; (ii) was insolvent or rendered insolvent by reason of such incurrence; (iii) was engaged in a business or transaction for which the guarantor's remaining assets constituted unreasonably small capital; or (iv) intended to incur, or believed that it would incur, debts beyond its ability to pay those debts as they mature. In addition, any payment by that guarantor under a guarantee could be voided and required to be returned to the guarantor or to a fund for the benefit of the creditors of the guarantor. The measures of insolvency for purposes of fraudulent transfer laws vary depending upon the governing law. Generally, a guarantor would be considered insolvent if: (i) the sum of its debts, including contingent liabilities, was greater than the fair saleable value of all of its assets; (ii) the present fair saleable value of its assets was less than the amount that would be required, to pay its probable liability on its existing debts, including contingent liabilities, as they become absolute and mature; or (iii) it could not pay its debts as they become due. Under Article 17 of the Bankruptcy (Désastre) (Jersey) Law 1990, as amended (the "Jersey Bankruptcy Law") and Article 176 of the Jersey Companies Law, the court may, on the application of the Viscount of Jersey (in the case of a company whose property has been declared "en désastre") or liquidator (in the case of a creditors' winding up, a procedure which is instigated by shareholders not creditors), set aside a guarantee entered into by a company with any person at an undervalue. There is a five year look back period from the date of commencement of the winding up or declaration of "désastre" during which guarantees are susceptible to examination pursuant to this rule. If the court determines that the transaction was a transaction at an undervalue, the court can make such order as it thinks fit to restore the position to what it would have been in if the transaction had not been entered into. In any proceedings, it is for the Viscount of Jersey or liquidator to demonstrate that the Jersey company was insolvent unless a beneficiary of the transaction was a connected person or associate of the company, in which case there is a presumption of insolvency and the connected person must demonstrate the Jersey company was not insolvent when it entered the transaction in such proceedings. Under Article 17A of the Jersey Bankruptcy Law and Article 176A of the Jersey Companies Law, the court may, on the application of the Viscount of Jersey (in the case of a company whose property has been declared "en désastre") or liquidator (in the case of a creditors' winding up), set aside a preference (including a guarantee) given by the company to any person. There is a 12 month look back period from the date of commencement of the winding up or declaration of "désastre" during which guarantees are susceptible to examination pursuant to this rule. A guarantee will constitute a preference if it has the effect of putting a creditor of the Jersey company (or a surety or guarantor for any of the company's debts or liabilities) in a better position (in the event of the company going into an insolvent winding up) than such creditor, guarantor or surety would otherwise have been in had that transaction not been entered into. If the court determines that the guarantee constituted such a preference, the court has very wide powers for restoring the position to what it would have been if that preference had not been given.

Under Article 17A of the Jersey Bankruptcy Law and Article 176A of the Jersey Companies Law, the court may, upon application by the Viscount of Jersey (in the case of a company whose property has been declared "en désastre") or the liquidator (in the case of a creditors' winding up), set aside a preference—such as a guarantee—given by the company to any individual. This applies within a 12-month look-back period beginning from the date of the commencement of the winding up or the declaration of "désastre," during which guarantees are subject to examination. A guarantee will be considered a preference if it places a creditor of the Jersey company—or a surety or guarantor for any of the company’s debts or liabilities—in a better position than they would have been had the transaction not occurred, in the event of the company’s insolvency. If the court finds that the guarantee constituted such a preference, it has broad powers to restore the financial position to what it would have been absent the preference. However, for such a restoration to occur, it must be proven that the company acted with a desire to produce the preferential effect. In proceedings, it is the responsibility of the Viscount of Jersey or the liquidator to establish that the company was insolvent at the relevant time and that it was motivated by a desire to create a preferential outcome, unless the beneficiary of the guarantee is a connected person, in which case there is a presumption that the company acted with such a desire, and the connected person must prove otherwise. In addition to these statutory provisions, Jersey customary law principles—such as a Pauline action—may also allow for the setting aside of asset dispositions intended to defeat creditor claims.
